words_text: So this is a compilation of me practicing some of my recent repertoire throughout the week. Obviously enough, it's very noticeable that there is this obnoxious buzzing sound in the background at all times. That sound is called a drone. You might wonder why the hell some people like me voluntarily choose to inflict this aural suffering both on my family and myself. But I'd like to explain why I use it so heavily, and why you also should consider trying it too.

words_text: Contrary to what people might think, its helpfulness doesn't have to do with manually comparing my pitch to the pitch of the drone mentally— in fact that's what I'm trying to avoid. The reason, rather, has more to do with sound quality: despite being like a deafening laser, this particular synthetic soundwave option on the app Tunable is most similar to that of soundwaves produced by string instruments. Because the soundwaves have similar nature, they will more directly interact and collide with each other, producing a more obvious third soundwave, which has its own frequency and pitch.

words_text: That third soundwave is called an overtone. Overtones are actually audible to us if you listen carefully, and its pitch and quality will change depending on its parent soundwave frequencies— aka us and the drone On the spectrum of all possible pitches to combine, including semitones most are dissonant with each other and have soundwaves that collide a lot when placed on top of each other— and we're talking about a collision every millionth of a second. As a result, the overtone that is produced by them has soundwaves that look like this and as you can perhaps intuitively infer from the shape, they kinda sound like wawawawa noise in the background.

words_text: However, like with any rule, there are exceptions. There's a very specific set of intervals where the overtone's frequency is an integer multiple of the parent frequencies, meaning the overtone's wave fits synergetically with the parent waves rather than constantly colliding with them. These instances are universally referred to as perfect intervals. The frequency of soundwaves in fifths have a 3:2 ratio, fourths have a 4:3 ratio, and octaves have a 2:1 ratio. So the overtone's wave they produce looks more like this which has a more diffused rather than distinct amplitude fluctuation, thus giving them their characteristic perfectly stable and pure sound.

words_text: The reason why this makes having a drone on helpful for training intonation is because since the intervals are perfect, your intonation also has to be perfect in order to produce the clear sound. Even being microscopically out of tune will produce the wacky dissonant overtones instead, indicating immediately to you that you have something to work on. Because I admittedly only have relative rather than perfect pitch, instead of just listening harder I'd 1000 prefer saving that mental energy and just react to wiggly sounds in the air. So yeah.
